title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 24
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Before the Brigade
passages.text:
A. Fire in a timber city was not an accident but a certainty, and the arrangements for dealing with it were correspondingly communal. Householders were required to keep buckets, ladders and hooks; neighbours were obliged to turn out; and the principal technique was not extinguishing the fire but pulling down the buildings in its path to deprive it of fuel. Demolition, not water, was the main instrument for centuries.

B. The first organised brigades were created by insurers rather than by cities, and their logic was strictly commercial. A company that had underwritten a building had an interest in that building not burning, and none in its neighbour. Insured premises carried a metal badge identifying the underwriter, and a brigade arriving at a fire established whose customer it was before deciding what to do — an arrangement that reads as absurd and followed directly from who was paying.

C. Municipal services replaced this because the commercial model failed at the thing that matters most about fire, which is that it spreads. A fire in an uninsured building becomes a fire in an insured one, and any brigade that ignores the first is failing its own customers. The economics pointed towards a single service covering everything regardless of who had paid, and the transfer to public provision followed the logic rather than any change in sentiment.

D. Water supply determined what any brigade could achieve for most of this history. Pumps were limited by what could be brought to them, and until pressurised mains existed a brigade's capacity was measured in how fast a chain of people could move buckets. The engineering that mattered was therefore municipal plumbing rather than fire equipment, and the sharpest reductions in urban fire loss followed the mains rather than the machines.

E. Prevention has always achieved more than response and has always attracted less attention. Building codes requiring separation, non-combustible materials and multiple exits removed most of the conditions that made historic fires catastrophic, and they did so invisibly, producing no incident to report. The measurable success of prevention is an absence, which is a persistent problem for anything funded by public enthusiasm.

F. The modern service has become something the name no longer describes. Most call-outs in high-income countries are not fires but medical emergencies, road collisions, flooding and rescues, a shift produced by the very prevention measures that made fire rarer. An organisation defined by a hazard it has largely designed out now spends most of its time on hazards nobody organised it around.

passages.title: The Shape of the Eye
passages.text:
Short-sightedness occurs when the eyeball grows slightly too long for its optical power, so that light focuses in front of the retina rather than on it. The defect is easily corrected and easily dismissed as trivial, and the reason it is taken seriously is that the elongation itself carries risk: a substantially longer eye is more prone to retinal detachment, glaucoma and macular problems in later life, and correction does not remove that.

The condition has become dramatically more common in a period far too short for genetic change to explain. In parts of East Asia the proportion of young adults affected has risen from a minority to the large majority within two generations, and comparable rises are visible in Europe and North America at a slower rate. Something in how children now live has changed the developing eye, and identifying what took longer than it should have.

The intuitive culprit was close work — reading, and more recently screens — and it turns out to be at most a secondary factor. Studies that controlled for time spent outdoors repeatedly found time outdoors the stronger predictor of the two, and children who read a great deal but also spend substantial time outside show much lower rates than the reading alone would predict. The association with study intensity is real and is largely an association with being indoors while studying.

The mechanism appears to be light intensity rather than distance of focus. Outdoor illumination is one to two orders of magnitude brighter than indoor lighting even on an overcast day, and bright light stimulates release of a signalling molecule in the retina that appears to slow axial elongation. This explains why the protective effect does not depend on what the child is doing outside, and why it cannot be replicated by ordinary indoor lighting.

Trials built on this have produced results unusual for their clarity. Adding a scheduled outdoor period to the school day reduces the incidence of new cases measurably, at essentially no cost, using no technology and requiring no compliance from the child beyond being outside. Few public health interventions have that combination, and its adoption has nonetheless been slow, since time outdoors competes directly with instruction in systems under pressure to raise attainment.

Treatment for children who are already affected has moved from correction to slowing progression. Specific spectacle and contact-lens designs, and low-concentration drops, reduce the rate at which the eye continues to elongate, and the aim is explicitly to limit final eye length rather than to sharpen vision, which glasses already do. The distinction between correcting a symptom and limiting the underlying change is the one most parents have never had explained to them.

passages.title: The Missing Houses
passages.text:
Housing costs in successful cities have risen faster than incomes for decades, and the explanations offered publicly tend to identify a villain rather than a mechanism. Foreign purchasers, empty investment properties, short-term lettings and speculation all appear in the argument, and all are real in specific places at specific scales. None is large enough to account for a pattern that appears in cities with entirely different ownership rules, tax systems and levels of foreign investment.

What those cities share is a constraint on adding homes where people want to live. Where the number of dwellings that may be built is limited by rules — height limits, minimum plot sizes, prohibitions on subdividing, procedural rights allowing existing residents to object — additional demand cannot produce additional supply and expresses itself entirely in price. This is unglamorous as a diagnosis and fits the evidence better than the alternatives.

The objections to building have a rational core that is frequently misrepresented by both sides. Existing residents face concentrated, immediate and visible costs — construction, congestion, changed views, pressure on schools and clinics — while the benefits are diffuse, delayed and largely accrue to people who do not yet live there and therefore cannot vote. A system that gives decision rights to the first group and none to the second will restrict building whatever anyone's stated intentions.

The claim that new construction raises local prices is the one that most needs disentangling. New buildings are usually expensive because building is expensive, and new arrivals in an area often precede visible construction, so the observed correlation is genuine. What the evidence supports is that adding homes lowers prices relative to what they would otherwise have been, both locally and across the wider market as households move into new stock and release older stock behind them.

Subsidised housing is necessary and is not a substitute for supply. Where the total number of dwellings is capped, a subsidised unit largely displaces a market unit, and the programme redistributes access rather than expanding it — help for those who receive it, no change to the aggregate shortage. Countries that have combined substantial social provision with permissive rules on total construction have achieved both; those that have tried subsidy alone have generally achieved a lottery.

The politics of this is genuinely hard and is not improved by pretending otherwise. Existing owners hold most of their wealth in the asset whose price would be moderated, and asking them to vote for that is asking a great deal. Reforms that have worked have generally moved decisions to a level of government where the beneficiaries are also represented, and have compensated the immediate costs rather than dismissing them as obstruction.
